paragraphs.heading: What the Himalayas are
paragraphs.text: The Himalayas are a mountain range in Asia. The range stands between the Tibetan Plateau and the plains of the Indian subcontinent. Some of Earth's highest peaks are here, among them the highest of all, Mount Everest. More than 100 peaks in the range rise above 7,200 metres (23,600 feet). Five countries share the range: Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan.

paragraphs.heading: How the range was lifted
paragraphs.text: The Himalayas were lifted up after the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. More exactly, the uppermost Indian crust folded, and that folding raised the mountains. Meanwhile a lower layer kept pushing on into Tibet and added thickness to its plateau. The still lower crust, together with the mantle, was subducted under Eurasia.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and size
paragraphs.text: The range forms an arc 2,400 km (1,500 mi) long, running from west-northwest to east-southeast. Its western anchor is Nanga Parbat, which stands a little south of the Indus River's northernmost bend. Its eastern anchor is Namcha Barwa, right to the west of the Yarlung Tsangpo River's great bend. The range is 350 kilometres wide in the west and 151 km wide in the east.

paragraphs.heading: Four ranges side by side
paragraphs.text: The Himalayas are made of four parallel mountain ranges. From south to north they are the Sivalik Hills, the Lower Himalayan Range, the Great Himalayas and the Tibetan Himalayas. The Great Himalayas are the highest and the central range. The Karakoram are generally treated as separate from the Himalayas.

paragraphs.heading: Borders and rivers
paragraphs.text: The Karakoram and Hindu Kush ranges border the Himalayas on the northwest. The Tibetan Plateau lies to the north and the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the south. The Indus, the Ganges and the Tsangpo–Brahmaputra, which are among the world's major rivers, rise near the Himalayas. About 600 million people live in the combined drainage basin of these rivers, and 53 million live in the Himalayas themselves.

paragraphs.heading: Giants of the central range
paragraphs.text: Midway along the range's great curve stand the 8,000 m peaks of Dhaulagiri and Annapurna in Nepal, with the Kali Gandaki Gorge between them. This gorge divides the Himalayas into a Western section and an Eastern section. The Mahalangur Himal holds four of the world's six highest mountains: Cho Oyu, Everest, Lhotse and Makalu.

paragraphs.heading: Sacred peaks
paragraphs.text: The Himalayas have deeply shaped the cultures of South Asia and Tibet. Many of the peaks are sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism, and the summits of several are closed to climbers. These include Gangkhar Puensum, Machapuchare and Nanda Devi. Gangkhar Puensum, the highest mountain in Bhutan, is also a strong candidate for the title of the world's highest unclimbed mountain.
